metadata.summary: Recognize Wernicke risk, distinguish preventive and treatment regimens, and rebuild nutrition through individualized goals and monitored feeding.
metadata.application: Treat neurological and glucose emergencies promptly, calculate the prescribed nutrition goal, and coordinate monitored feeding and recovery follow-up.
keyPoints: A missing classic finding does not exclude Wernicke encephalopathy.
A preventive thiamine dose does not establish adequate neurological treatment.
Urgent glucose must not wait for thiamine.
An eventual calorie goal is not a first-day refeeding prescription.

bodies.heading: Recognize risk before the full triad appears
bodies.body: Thiamine deficiency can injure the brain in people with prolonged poor intake and alcohol dependence, including those who are still drinking. Confusion, gait ataxia and abnormal eye movements are important Wernicke encephalopathy findings, but absence of one finding does not exclude the condition. New confusion with malnutrition or ataxia warrants urgent assessment and parenteral thiamine when Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected. Evaluate hypoglycemia, withdrawal, HE, infection, medicines and other neurological causes at the same time; do not attribute every altered mental state to one liver diagnosis or wait for all three classic findings.

bodies.heading: Separate prevention from neurological treatment
bodies.body: The route and regimen depend on the purpose, nutritional risk and ability to absorb oral treatment. ASAM withdrawal guidance prefers IV or IM thiamine for poor nutrition, malabsorption or severe withdrawal complications and describes a typical preventive regimen of 100 mg IV or IM daily for 3 to 5 days; oral thiamine can also be offered in appropriate circumstances. This preventive example is not an adequate-treatment rule for newly suspected Wernicke encephalopathy. Other hospital guidance uses higher preventive doses for high-risk patients. Follow the relevant hospital protocol and reassess risk and symptoms rather than applying one dose to every patient.

bodies.heading: Treat suspected Wernicke encephalopathy promptly
bodies.body: Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy requires hospital care and a parenteral treatment regimen, usually IV, with daily neurological review. As one clearly identified treatment example, UK alcohol-care guidance published in 2025 recommends IV thiamine 300 to 500 mg three times daily for 3 to 5 days, with further parenteral therapy when symptoms persist and improvement continues. NICE CG100 recommends at least 5 days of parenteral treatment unless Wernicke encephalopathy is excluded, followed by oral thiamine. These are purpose-specific guideline examples, not instructions to combine protocols or stop automatically on day 3. Use the treating service’s regimen, assess competing causes and administer parenteral therapy where trained staff can manage hypersensitivity reactions.

bodies.heading: Do not delay urgent glucose
bodies.body: Symptomatic hypoglycemia needs prompt glucose treatment. ASAM permits glucose and thiamine in either order or concurrently; waiting for a thiamine dose must not postpone urgently needed glucose. Give thiamine promptly as well, particularly when malnutrition or Wernicke risk is present. Thiamine is not a substitute for glucose, and correcting the glucose value does not complete vitamin or nutrition care. For planned feeding, arrange thiamine support before and during nutrition when feasible under the refeeding protocol, while keeping emergency hypoglycemia treatment immediate.

bodies.heading: Correct electrolyte partners with monitoring
bodies.body: Check and recheck magnesium when Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected: low magnesium can impair activation and effectiveness of thiamine. Correct documented deficiency with the treating team and monitor kidney function and the clinical response. Review potassium and phosphate as well, especially during nutrition initiation. Replacement dose, route and monitoring depend on severity, renal function and the care setting. This is a reason to identify and treat deficiencies, not to administer unrestricted magnesium to every patient or to stop thiamine because early improvement is incomplete.

bodies.heading: Assess nutrition beyond the albumin value
bodies.body: Assess current intake, recent weight change, fluid retention, muscle loss, function and the ability to swallow and obtain food. Involve a dietitian and address nausea, confusion and other barriers to eating. Ascites and edema can distort measured weight; low albumin reflects disease and does not independently measure protein intake or nutritional recovery. Thiamine, vitamin B12 and zinc deficits are common in alcohol-associated hepatitis; evaluate and replete clinically relevant deficiencies. Vitamins and minerals do not provide the calories and protein needed to rebuild reserve, and a generic supplement list does not establish a safe dose for every patient.

bodies.heading: Calculate a qualified nutrition goal
bodies.body: ACG recommends a goal of 35 kcal/kg/day and 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day of protein for alcohol-associated hepatitis. AASLD adult cirrhosis guidance also recommends 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day of protein and uses ideal body weight pragmatically for protein calculations; energy needs depend on the patient, body composition and illness. For a worked non-obese example, assume the dietitian has selected 70 kg as the appropriate weight for both prescribed calculations: 35 × 70 = 2,450 kcal/day, and 1.2 × 70 to 1.5 × 70 = 84 to 105 g protein/day. This is the eventual prescribed goal, not an automatic first-day feed in a depleted patient. Fluid overload, obesity, critical illness, kidney disease and measured energy expenditure can require a different individualized plan.

bodies.heading: Preserve protein and shorten fasting
bodies.body: Do not routinely restrict protein because a patient with cirrhosis has HE. Maintain the individualized protein goal while treating HE and its precipitants; restriction can worsen muscle catabolism. Encourage varied protein sources, including vegetable and dairy foods, rather than imposing a universal meat ban. Small meals or snacks about every 3 to 4 waking hours and an early breakfast or late-evening snack can reduce long fasting periods. Match the snack and meal plan to intake needs and tolerance; branched-chain amino acid products are not a universal substitute for adequate daily protein.

bodies.heading: Recognize and monitor refeeding risk
bodies.body: Prolonged negligible intake, substantial weight loss and low phosphate, potassium or magnesium before feeding identify refeeding risk. NICE includes little or no intake for more than 10 days or low baseline electrolytes among its high-risk criteria. Use a trained nutrition team and the relevant refeeding protocol to select the initial intake and advance it with monitoring, rather than immediately delivering the eventual full calorie target. Provide thiamine and appropriate micronutrients, assess fluid balance and check electrolytes, glucose and kidney function at baseline and frequently during initiation; NICE recommends daily phosphate and magnesium checks when refeeding risk is present, with frequency adapted to clinical instability. New weakness, an arrhythmia, worsening fluid overload or falling phosphate needs prompt assessment and correction, not automatic feed escalation. Refeeding problems can occur with oral, enteral or parenteral nutrition.

bodies.heading: Escalate support and assign follow-up
bodies.body: When safe oral intake cannot meet the plan, add oral nutritional supplements and measure whether intake improves. For alcohol-associated hepatitis, ACG recommends enteral nutrition when oral intake remains inadequate despite supplements. The team should assess gastrointestinal function, swallowing and airway safety, hemodynamic stability and suitable access; ALD alone does not mandate parenteral nutrition or exclude enteral feeding. Plan nutrition support through the appropriate service when the gastrointestinal route is insufficient or unusable. Before discharge, assign follow-up for intake, weight interpreted with fluid status, electrolytes, vitamin therapy and access to food alongside continuing liver and AUD care. Completion of withdrawal is not completion of recovery treatment.

check.question: A malnourished adult with alcohol dependence is confused and has symptomatic hypoglycemia. IV glucose is ready, but thiamine has not yet arrived. Which action is best?
choices: Treat the hypoglycemia promptly and administer thiamine as soon as possible.
Wait for thiamine before giving any glucose, despite the symptomatic hypoglycemia.
Give thiamine alone because it directly replaces the missing glucose.
Give glucose now and omit further thiamine assessment because glucose correction excludes Wernicke risk.
check.rationale: Treat symptomatic hypoglycemia without delay. ASAM permits glucose and thiamine in either order or concurrently, so waiting for thiamine must not postpone emergency glucose. Give thiamine promptly as well. Thiamine does not replace glucose, and glucose correction does not remove the patient’s nutritional or Wernicke risk.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-045.question: A patient with alcohol dependence, weeks of poor intake and new confusion has an unsteady gait but no documented eye-movement abnormality. Which response is best?
choices: Urgently assess suspected Wernicke encephalopathy and give protocol-directed parenteral thiamine while evaluating other causes.
Exclude Wernicke encephalopathy because all three classic findings are not present.
Treat presumed HE alone and wait for persistent eye findings before considering thiamine.
Use an oral multivitamin as the sole response to the new neurological findings.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-045.rationale: Confusion with poor nutrition and ataxia supports urgent Wernicke assessment even without ocular findings. Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy needs parenteral thiamine and clinical review in hospital. The full triad is not required; HE, withdrawal, hypoglycemia and other causes should be evaluated concurrently rather than replacing vitamin treatment with one presumed diagnosis. An oral multivitamin alone is not the neurological treatment regimen.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-046.question: A malnourished adult with alcohol dependence has a glucose of 38 mg/dL, sweating and confusion. IV access and glucose are available, but the thiamine dose is being prepared. What is the best sequence?
choices: Give urgent glucose now and administer thiamine promptly, in either order or concurrently as feasible.
Withhold glucose until thiamine is administered, regardless of the hypoglycemic symptoms.
Give thiamine alone and wait for it to correct the low glucose.
Correct the glucose and permanently omit thiamine because the patient no longer has vitamin-deficiency risk.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-046.rationale: The symptomatic glucose of 38 mg/dL requires immediate treatment. ASAM permits glucose and thiamine in either order or concurrently, so emergency glucose must not wait. Thiamine should still be given promptly according to risk and purpose; it is not a glucose substitute. Correcting hypoglycemia does not erase malnutrition or Wernicke risk.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-047.question: A hospitalized patient was receiving thiamine 100 mg IV daily for withdrawal prophylaxis but now develops confusion and gait ataxia. Which interpretation is best?
choices: Reassess urgently for Wernicke encephalopathy and move to the hospital’s parenteral treatment pathway if suspected.
The preventive 100 mg daily regimen guarantees adequate treatment of any newly developing Wernicke encephalopathy.
Switch to an oral multivitamin alone because new neurological findings prove parenteral thiamine is unnecessary.
Stop thiamine because prevention and treatment always use an identical regimen.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-047.rationale: ASAM describes 100 mg IV or IM daily for 3 to 5 days as a typical preventive withdrawal regimen, not a guarantee of adequate neurological treatment. New confusion and ataxia require urgent assessment, competing-cause evaluation and purpose-specific parenteral treatment when Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected. Oral multivitamins alone do not replace that pathway, and prevention and treatment are not interchangeable.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-048.question: During parenteral treatment for suspected Wernicke encephalopathy, a patient has documented hypomagnesemia and incomplete early neurological improvement. Which action is most appropriate?
choices: Continue clinical reassessment and thiamine treatment while correcting low magnesium with renal and electrolyte monitoring.
Declare thiamine ineffective and stop it without reviewing magnesium or competing causes.
Give unrestricted magnesium to every patient regardless of the value or kidney function.
Wait until a fixed thiamine course ends before assessing the documented magnesium deficiency.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-048.rationale: Magnesium supports conversion of thiamine to its active form, and hypomagnesemia can impair response. Recheck and correct the documented deficiency while continuing appropriate thiamine treatment and reviewing other causes. Replacement must account for kidney function, severity and monitoring; neither unrestricted magnesium nor delaying assessment until a fixed course ends is appropriate.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-093.question: For a non-obese patient with alcohol-associated hepatitis, the dietitian selects 70 kg for both calculations and prescribes an eventual goal of 35 kcal/kg/day plus 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day protein. Which daily goal matches that prescription?
choices: 2,450 kcal and 84 to 105 g protein.
2,450 kcal and 42 to 52.5 g protein.
3,500 kcal and 84 to 105 g protein.
2,450 kcal and 120 to 150 g protein.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-093.rationale: Energy is 35 kcal/kg × 70 kg = 2,450 kcal/day. Protein is 1.2 × 70 = 84 g through 1.5 × 70 = 105 g/day. The other options halve protein, use 100 kg for energy or omit the prescribed weight in the protein calculation. These are the eventual goals for the stated individualized prescription; refeeding risk can require a lower initial intake and monitored advancement.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-094.question: A patient with cirrhosis and HE has poor intake and muscle loss. Which nutrition plan best follows adult cirrhosis guidance?
choices: Maintain an individualized protein goal while treating HE, addressing intake barriers and reducing prolonged fasting.
Remove all protein until an ammonia result returns to the reference range.
Use routine severe protein restriction as the primary strategy for restoring muscle.
Ban all animal protein in every patient and replace the full nutrition plan with a vitamin tablet.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-094.rationale: AASLD recommends adequate individualized protein and no routine protein restriction for HE. Restriction can worsen muscle catabolism; HE treatment and nutritional support should proceed together. Use varied sources, including vegetable and dairy protein, with small frequent meals and a suitable late snack or early breakfast. Ammonia is not a gate for resuming all protein, a universal meat ban is not required, and vitamins cannot replace calories and protein.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-095.question: A patient has taken almost no food for 12 days and has low phosphate before feeding. After nutrition starts, phosphate falls further and new weakness develops. Which response is best?
choices: Promptly assess possible refeeding problems, correct deficiencies and reassess feed advancement under a monitored nutrition protocol.
Immediately increase intake to the full eventual calorie goal without electrolyte review.
Use albumin alone to decide that the feed is safe despite the phosphate trend and weakness.
Exclude refeeding problems because the nutrition is enteral rather than parenteral.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-095.rationale: More than 10 days of negligible intake and low baseline phosphate identify high refeeding risk in NICE CG32. Falling phosphate and new weakness require prompt clinical and electrolyte assessment, correction and review of feeding advancement. Provide thiamine and monitor other electrolytes, glucose, kidney function and fluid status. Albumin alone cannot establish nutrition safety, and oral or enteral feeding does not eliminate refeeding risk.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-096.question: A patient with alcohol-associated hepatitis still cannot meet nutrition needs despite oral supplements. The gastrointestinal tract is usable, and the team has assessed airway safety, stability and access. Which next step best follows ACG guidance?
choices: Arrange an individualized enteral nutrition plan with the nutrition team.
Use parenteral nutrition automatically because alcohol-associated hepatitis excludes gastrointestinal feeding.
Replace calorie and protein support with larger vitamin doses alone.
Continue the inadequate intake indefinitely because starting oral supplements proves nutrition needs are met.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-096.rationale: ACG recommends enteral nutrition for alcohol-associated hepatitis when oral intake remains inadequate despite supplements. The route requires individual assessment, including gastrointestinal function, airway safety, stability and access. ALD alone does not require parenteral nutrition; vitamins do not replace macronutrients, and a supplement order must be followed by assessment of actual intake.

choices: Reassess urgently for Wernicke encephalopathy and move to the hospital’s parenteral treatment pathway if suspected.
The preventive 100 mg daily regimen guarantees adequate treatment of any newly developing Wernicke encephalopathy.
Switch to an oral multivitamin alone because new neurological findings prove parenteral thiamine is unnecessary.
Stop thiamine because prevention and treatment always use an identical regimen.
wholeObject.rationale: ASAM describes 100 mg IV or IM daily for 3 to 5 days as a typical preventive withdrawal regimen, not a guarantee of adequate neurological treatment. New confusion and ataxia require urgent assessment, competing-cause evaluation and purpose-specific parenteral treatment when Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected. Oral multivitamins alone do not replace that pathway, and prevention and treatment are not interchangeable.

wholeChoiceReview: Correct: new signs warrant urgent treatment-pathway reassessment.
False: a preventive 100 mg regimen does not guarantee adequate neurological therapy.
False: oral multivitamin alone not indicated neurological regimen.
False: purposes and regimens are not interchangeable.

wholeObject.question: During parenteral treatment for suspected Wernicke encephalopathy, a patient has documented hypomagnesemia and incomplete early neurological improvement. Which action is most appropriate?
choices: Continue clinical reassessment and thiamine treatment while correcting low magnesium with renal and electrolyte monitoring.
Declare thiamine ineffective and stop it without reviewing magnesium or competing causes.
Give unrestricted magnesium to every patient regardless of the value or kidney function.
Wait until a fixed thiamine course ends before assessing the documented magnesium deficiency.
wholeObject.rationale: Magnesium supports conversion of thiamine to its active form, and hypomagnesemia can impair response. Recheck and correct the documented deficiency while continuing appropriate thiamine treatment and reviewing other causes. Replacement must account for kidney function, severity and monitoring; neither unrestricted magnesium nor delaying assessment until a fixed course ends is appropriate.

wholeChoiceReview: Correct: continue clinical/thiamine review and correct documented low Mg safely.
False: no unreviewed stopping because response incomplete.
False: renal and level-dependent dosing required.
False: documented deficit needs timely review, not arbitrary end-course delay.

wholeObject.question: For a non-obese patient with alcohol-associated hepatitis, the dietitian selects 70 kg for both calculations and prescribes an eventual goal of 35 kcal/kg/day plus 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day protein. Which daily goal matches that prescription?
choices: 2,450 kcal and 84 to 105 g protein.
2,450 kcal and 42 to 52.5 g protein.
3,500 kcal and 84 to 105 g protein.
2,450 kcal and 120 to 150 g protein.
wholeObject.rationale: Energy is 35 kcal/kg × 70 kg = 2,450 kcal/day. Protein is 1.2 × 70 = 84 g through 1.5 × 70 = 105 g/day. The other options halve protein, use 100 kg for energy or omit the prescribed weight in the protein calculation. These are the eventual goals for the stated individualized prescription; refeeding risk can require a lower initial intake and monitored advancement.

wholeChoiceReview: False: protein is halved.
False: energy wrongly uses 100 kg.
False: protein fails to use prescribed 70 kg, yielding 120–150 instead of 84–105.

wholeObject.question: A patient with cirrhosis and HE has poor intake and muscle loss. Which nutrition plan best follows adult cirrhosis guidance?
choices: Maintain an individualized protein goal while treating HE, addressing intake barriers and reducing prolonged fasting.
Remove all protein until an ammonia result returns to the reference range.
Use routine severe protein restriction as the primary strategy for restoring muscle.
Ban all animal protein in every patient and replace the full nutrition plan with a vitamin tablet.
wholeObject.rationale: AASLD recommends adequate individualized protein and no routine protein restriction for HE. Restriction can worsen muscle catabolism; HE treatment and nutritional support should proceed together. Use varied sources, including vegetable and dairy protein, with small frequent meals and a suitable late snack or early breakfast. Ammonia is not a gate for resuming all protein, a universal meat ban is not required, and vitamins cannot replace calories and protein.

wholeChoiceReview: Correct: individualized protein, HE treatment, barriers and fasting addressed.
False: no ammonia gate for eliminating all protein.
False: routine severe restriction worsens muscle catabolism.
False: universal meat ban and vitamin-only substitution unsupported.

Use varied sources, including vegetable and dairy protein, with small frequent meals and a suitable late snack or early breakfast. Ammonia is not a gate for resuming all protein, a universal meat ban is not required, and vitamins cannot replace calories and protein.

wholeObject.question: A patient has taken almost no food for 12 days and has low phosphate before feeding. After nutrition starts, phosphate falls further and new weakness develops. Which response is best?
choices: Promptly assess possible refeeding problems, correct deficiencies and reassess feed advancement under a monitored nutrition protocol.
Immediately increase intake to the full eventual calorie goal without electrolyte review.
Use albumin alone to decide that the feed is safe despite the phosphate trend and weakness.
Exclude refeeding problems because the nutrition is enteral rather than parenteral.
wholeObject.rationale: More than 10 days of negligible intake and low baseline phosphate identify high refeeding risk in NICE CG32. Falling phosphate and new weakness require prompt clinical and electrolyte assessment, correction and review of feeding advancement. Provide thiamine and monitor other electrolytes, glucose, kidney function and fluid status. Albumin alone cannot establish nutrition safety, and oral or enteral feeding does not eliminate refeeding risk.

wholeChoiceReview: Correct: high-risk pattern/falling phosphate/weakness warrants assessment/correction/advancement review.
False: full-goal escalation without review unsafe.
False: albumin alone does not establish safety.
False: refeeding can occur with enteral nutrition.

Albumin alone cannot establish nutrition safety, and oral or enteral feeding does not eliminate refeeding risk.

wholeObject.question: A patient with alcohol-associated hepatitis still cannot meet nutrition needs despite oral supplements. The gastrointestinal tract is usable, and the team has assessed airway safety, stability and access. Which next step best follows ACG guidance?
choices: Arrange an individualized enteral nutrition plan with the nutrition team.
Use parenteral nutrition automatically because alcohol-associated hepatitis excludes gastrointestinal feeding.
Replace calorie and protein support with larger vitamin doses alone.
Continue the inadequate intake indefinitely because starting oral supplements proves nutrition needs are met.
wholeObject.rationale: ACG recommends enteral nutrition for alcohol-associated hepatitis when oral intake remains inadequate despite supplements. The route requires individual assessment, including gastrointestinal function, airway safety, stability and access. ALD alone does not require parenteral nutrition; vitamins do not replace macronutrients, and a supplement order must be followed by assessment of actual intake.

wholeChoiceReview: Correct: AH persistent inadequate ONS with suitable gut/safety leads to individualized EN.
False: ALD alone does not mandate PN or exclude EN.
False: vitamins cannot supply calories/protein.
False: supplementation order does not establish adequacy.
